vopros: I run a small service business in Los Angeles and customers keep haggling on price. Who in LA can help me with that?

vyzhimka.tekst:
Yes. For a small LA service business, I’d look for help with both pricing strategy and sales/negotiation—not just a generic business coach. Repeated haggling can mean the issue is how the price is presented, how the service is packaged, or which customers you're attracting.

A few LA options worth considering:

- LA Regional SBDC Network — probably where I’d start. They provide no-cost, confidential one-on-one advising to small businesses in the LA region. Ask specifically for someone experienced in service-business pricing, margins, and sales. ([smallbizla.org](https://smallbizla.org/?utm_source=openai))
- SCORE Los Angeles — also free. They can match you with an experienced business mentor, including people with sales, marketing, and financial backgrounds. Mentoring can be ongoing rather than a one-off session. ([score.org](https://www.score.org/ca/los-angeles/?utm_source=openai))
- Lapin Negotiation Services — a West LA firm offering negotiation coaching and training. This is more appropriate if your prices/margins already make sense, but you or your employees are having trouble holding the line when customers push back. ([lapinnegotiationservices.com](https://lapinnegotiationservices.com/negotiation-services-los-angeles/?utm_source=openai))
- A specialized pricing consultant — potentially worthwhile once you have enough revenue that a modest improvement in average ticket materially affects profit. For example, firms such as Price to Profit specifically work on price increases and negotiation, although they're not necessarily the inexpensive/local-small-business option. ([price2profits.com](https://www.price2profits.com/services?utm_source=openai))

I wouldn't immediately pay thousands for a consultant. Start with LA SBDC and bring them your last 20–30 estimates: quoted price, service, whether the customer negotiated, final price, whether you won/lost the job, job cost, and approximate profit. That's enough to diagnose whether you're underpriced, attracting price shoppers, or simply conceding too easily.

If you tell me what kind of service business you run (e.g. cleaning, landscaping, photography, contractor, consulting) and roughly what customers typically spend ($200, $2,000, $20,000, etc.), I can narrow this down to the kind of LA advisor I'd use and what I'd ask them to fix.
